Papua New Guinea.text: Its most widely used language, Tok Pisin, is an English-based creole with some German words, from colonial times.
Papua New Guinea.evidence: Tok Pisin is an English-based creole language spoken throughout Papua New Guinea. It is an official language of Papua New Guinea and the most widely used language in the country. ... Tok Pisin derives some vocabulary from German as a result of this influence.

Indonesia.text: Javanese, not Indonesian, is the most common mother tongue (about 32% of people), though over 97% are fluent in Indonesian.
Indonesia.evidence: According to the 2020 census, over 97% of Indonesians are fluent in Indonesian. ... Javanese is the most spoken indigenous language, with native speakers constituting 31.8% of the total population of Indonesia

Nigeria.text: Its most common lingua franca is Nigerian Pidgin, an English-based creole spoken by over 60 million people.
Nigeria.evidence: The English-based creole Nigerian Pidgin ... has now become the most common lingua franca, spoken by over 60 million people.

India.text: Its rupee notes write their value in 17 languages, on a panel on the back.
India.evidence: Currency notes have 17 languages on the panel which appears on the reverse of the notes.

China.text: Its Chinese languages differ as much as English, German and Danish do, but all their speakers learn to write in Mandarin at school.
China.evidence: They differ as much from each other morphologically and phonetically as do English, German and Danish, but speakers of different Chinese languages are taught to write in Mandarin (written vernacular Mandarin) at school

Mexico.text: Its constitution names no official language, mostly out of respect for indigenous peoples, yet it is the largest Spanish-speaking country.
Mexico.evidence: The Constitution of Mexico does not declare an official language ... This makes Mexico the largest Spanish speaking country in the world. ... it has yet to declare it the national language mostly out of respect to the indigenous communities that still exist.

Cameroon.text: Ruled by both France and Britain until 1961, it has French and English as official languages, and a street mix of the two: Camfranglais.
Cameroon.evidence: French and English are official languages, a heritage of Cameroon's colonial past as a colony of both France and the United Kingdom from 1916 to 1961. ... Camfranglais (or Frananglais) is a relatively new pidgin communication form emerging in urban areas and other locations where Anglophone and Francophone Cameroonians meet and interact.

Australia.text: Of more than 250 Aboriginal languages, only about 100 are still spoken, and only 13 are still learned by children.
Australia.evidence: There are more than 250 distinct languages. ... In 2020, 90 percent of the barely more than 100 languages still spoken are considered endangered. Thirteen languages are still being acquired by children.

United States.text: Congress has never declared an official language; a 2025 executive order made it English.
United States.evidence: Congress has never declared a statutory official language, the federal government primarily uses English and a 2025 executive order declared English official.

Brazil.text: Besides Portuguese it has over 200 indigenous languages; Nheengatu, a descendant of Tupi, is official in São Gabriel da Cachoeira, German dialects in nine southern towns.
Brazil.evidence: Aside from Portuguese, the country also has numerous minority languages, including over 200 different indigenous languages, such as Nheengatu (a descendant of Tupi) ... In some municipalities, those minor languages have official status: Nheengatu, for example, is an official language in São Gabriel da Cachoeira, while a number of German dialects are official in nine southern municipalities.
